title: what it is and isn't
hook: what it is and isn't; a crown you tie yourself

segments.voice: Yesterday: naam japna, keeping the name. Your line was the three pillars: work, share, remember. Did you touch all three? Day twelve.

Early morning, in homes all over the world, someone stands in front of a mirror with a long strip of cloth, several meters of it. They hold one end in their teeth, and wrap, and fold, and tuck, layer by layer, the same way they did yesterday and will tomorrow. Ten minutes, maybe less if they've been doing it for years. It's one of the most recognizable sights in the world, and one of the most misunderstood. People have mistaken it for a costume, for a sign of some other faith, or for something to be afraid of. Today, what the Sikh turban is, and what it isn't.
screen: `A MIRROR, A LONG STRIP OF CLOTH.` → `WRAP, FOLD, TUCK.` → `RECOGNIZED, AND MISUNDERSTOOD.`

segments.voice: In Punjabi the turban is often called the dastar, a respectful word, or simply the pag. Start with what's underneath. Many Sikhs keep their hair uncut, all their lives, as a way of accepting the body as it was made. The turban covers and protects that hair. So it isn't a hat you take on and off with the weather. It's part of a commitment. Now the history. In the Gurus' time, in that part of the world, a fine turban was a sign of rank: kings and nobles wore them, and ordinary people often weren't expected to. The tenth Guru, Guru Gobind Singh, whom you'll meet properly in a few days, made the turban part of the identity of his community. The effect was deliberate: every Sikh, whoever their family was, wears a crown. Sikhs often describe it just like that. A crown you tie yourself, every morning. Many Sikh women wear one too; other Sikh women cover their hair with a scarf. And not every Sikh wears a turban. Some keep their hair and some don't, and Sikhs have real conversations about that. The scripture doesn't reduce faith to clothing. But for those who wear it, the turban does something else as well: it makes you visible. There's a teaching that a Sikh should be easy to find in a crowd, so that anyone in trouble knows where to turn. You can't hide in a turban. And what it isn't: it isn't a sign of any other religion, it isn't a costume, and it isn't a threat. Sikhs have sometimes been mistaken and even targeted because of it, which is why many communities hold turban-tying days for their neighbors, to explain.
screen: `THE DASTAR COVERS UNCUT HAIR.` · `ONCE A SIGN OF KINGS.` · `EVERY SIKH WEARS A CROWN.` · `YOU CAN'T HIDE IN A TURBAN.` · then, large: `A CROWN YOU TIE YOURSELF.`

segments.voice: Sit up, and let the crown of your head rise a little, as if something light and precious were resting there. Feel your spine lengthen underneath it. Breathe. Imagine walking into your day this way: not proud, just visible, steady, someone others could turn to if they needed help. Hold that posture. The bell holds the time.
The turban, the dastar. It covers uncut hair, marks a commitment, and makes every Sikh who wears it a crowned, visible person. Twelfth word.
Your line: carry yourself like it. Today, walk into one room as if you were wearing a crown: head up, steady, easy to find if someone needs you. Day twelve.

howItsDone: Many Sikhs tie a turban fresh each morning to cover their uncut hair; men and many women wear them, and others cover their hair with a scarf. Everyone covers their head in the gurdwara.

original.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi script: dastar, a respectful word for the turban; it comes from Persian.

trapdoor: what you thought: a religious hat.
what it means: a covering for uncut hair, tied fresh each day: a crown, and a way of being visible.
what a scholar hears: dastar is a Persian loanword. in the Gurus' era turbans marked rank, so a whole community wearing them was a statement of equal dignity.

notes: Sensitive topic: the script says not every Sikh wears a turban and 'Sikhs have real conversations about that' without taking a side. Keepers may want different wording (the Rehat Maryada requires kesh for amritdhari Sikhs).
'A teaching that a Sikh should be easy to find in a crowd, so that anyone in trouble knows where to turn' is a common modern explanation; confirm or soften to 'Sikhs often say'.
Turbans as a sign of rank in the Mughal era; confirm the historical framing.
Hate crimes are mentioned only generally ('mistaken and even targeted'); the Balbir Singh Sodhi story is on day 320.
